headline: petrichor
lesson: Petrichor was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists. It joins the Greek words for stone and for the fluid said to run in the veins of the gods.

headline: serendipity
lesson: Horace Walpole made the word up in 1754. He took it from a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept finding things they were not looking for.

headline: mellifluous
lesson: From the Latin mel, honey, and fluere, to flow. Use it for a voice or a tune so smooth and sweet that it seems to pour.

headline: ephemeral
lesson: From the Greek ephemeros, lasting a day. In English it was first used for fevers, and for insects that live for a single day, like the mayfly.

headline: defenestrate
lesson: From the Latin fenestra, window. The word is tied to Prague, where officials were thrown from a castle window in 1618, helping to start the Thirty Years War.

headline: apricity
lesson: A rare word recorded in a dictionary of 1623 and hardly used since. It is waiting for the next cold bright day when you turn your face to the sun.

headline: susurrus
lesson: From the Latin for a murmur or a whisper. Say it slowly and it does what it means: wind in dry leaves, or a quiet tide on sand.

headline: halcyon
lesson: The halcyon was a bird of Greek myth, said to nest on the sea and calm the waves. Halcyon days are a peaceful time you look back on fondly.

headline: ineffable
lesson: From the Latin for unutterable. It is the word for a feeling or a sight so big that language runs out, which makes it a word about the limits of words.

headline: overmorrow
lesson: English once had a single word for this, and German still does. Overmorrow fell out of use centuries ago, but nothing stops you bringing it back.

headline: tsundoku
lesson: A Japanese word that blends tsunde oku, to pile things up for later, with doku, reading. Most readers have a small tower of tsundoku somewhere.

headline: komorebi
lesson: A Japanese word with no single match in English. It is built from the words for tree, for leaking through and for sun.

headline: saudade
lesson: A Portuguese word for missing a person, a place or a time, mixed with the warmth of having known it. It is often called impossible to translate.

headline: hygge
lesson: A Danish and Norwegian word for the feeling of a warm room, good company and nothing to rush for. English borrowed it in the 2010s.

headline: sonorous
lesson: From the Latin sonor, sound. A church bell is sonorous. So is a cello, and so is the voice of someone reading aloud well.

headline: lethologica
lesson: The name for that moment when a word is on the tip of your tongue. It comes from the Greek lethe, forgetfulness, and logos, word.

headline: quixotic
lesson: From Don Quixote, the hero of the 1605 novel by Cervantes, who rode out to fight windmills that he believed were giants.

headline: sesquipedalian
lesson: From a Latin joke by the poet Horace about words a foot and a half long. It is a long word for long words, so it describes itself.

headline: eloquent
lesson: From the Latin loqui, to speak. Being eloquent is not about long words. It is about saying a thing so it lands with the person listening.

headline: luminous
lesson: From the Latin lumen, light. Paint can be luminous, and so can a watch dial, a jellyfish or a face with good news.

headline: muscle
lesson: The Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like a small mouse moving under the skin. The Latin word musculus means exactly that.

headline: disaster
lesson: From the Italian disastro: dis, bad, and astro, star. People once blamed calamities on the unlucky position of a planet or a star.

headline: goodbye
lesson: Over the 1500s the phrase was squeezed into godbwye. The first part then shifted to good, copying good day and good night.

headline: clue
lesson: A clew was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth Theseus used one to find his way out of the Labyrinth, so a clew came to mean anything that guides you to an answer.

headline: window
lesson: From the Old Norse vindauga: vindr, wind, and auga, eye. Early windows were plain openings in a wall or roof that let smoke out and wind in.

headline: daisy
lesson: The Old English name was the day’s eye, because the flower opens its petals at dawn and closes them again at dusk.

headline: companion
lesson: From the Latin com, with, and panis, bread. A companion was the person you broke bread with. Company comes from the same root.

headline: robot
lesson: It first appeared in a Czech play of 1920 about factory-made workers. The writer’s brother suggested the word, from robota.

headline: quarantine
lesson: From the Venetian quaranta giorni. During the plague, ships arriving in Venice had to wait at anchor for forty days before anyone could come ashore.

headline: nice
lesson: From the Latin nescius, not knowing. Over seven centuries the word drifted from silly to fussy to precise, and only then to pleasant.

headline: silly
lesson: In Old English it meant happy or blessed. It slid to innocent, then to pitiable, then to weak, and at last to foolish.

headline: nightmare
lesson: A mare was an evil spirit in old folklore, said to sit on the chests of sleepers and bring bad dreams.

headline: whisky
lesson: From the Gaelic uisge beatha. English speakers wore the phrase down over time until only whisky was left.

headline: checkmate
lesson: Shah mat travelled with the game of chess through Arabic and French into English. Shah, king, also gives us the word check.

headline: algebra
lesson: Al-jabr comes from the title of a book written in Baghdad around the year 820 by al-Khwarizmi, whose own name gave us the word algorithm.

headline: sarcasm
lesson: The Greek sarkazein meant to strip off flesh like a dog, then to bite the lip in rage, then to sneer. Sharp words have always had teeth.

headline: tragedy
lesson: From the Greek tragos, goat, and oide, song. Nobody is sure why. A goat may have been the prize in early Athenian drama contests.

headline: candidate
lesson: In ancient Rome, men standing for office wore a toga rubbed bright white with chalk. The Latin candidus, shining white, also gives us candid.

headline: shampoo
lesson: Champo first meant a massage. The word reached Britain in the 1700s and only came to mean washing hair about a century later.

headline: emoji
lesson: It is Japanese: e, picture, and moji, character. The likeness to the English word emoticon is a happy accident.

headline: Brevity is the soul of wit.
lesson: The joke is on the speaker. Polonius says this in the middle of a long, rambling speech, and Shakespeare lets the audience notice.

headline: Words, words, words.
lesson: Polonius asks Hamlet what he is reading, and this is the whole reply. Three words that say he is tired of being watched and tired of empty talk.

headline: The pen is mightier than the sword.
lesson: The idea is far older, but this is the wording that stuck. Almost everybody knows the line and almost nobody remembers who wrote it.

headline: Language is the dress of thought.
lesson: Johnson wrote one of the first great English dictionaries, published in 1755. He believed that how you say a thing shapes how it is heard.

headline: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
lesson: A philosopher’s way of saying that every new word you learn makes your world a little bigger.

headline: Curiouser and curiouser!
connecting: Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
lesson: Alice is so surprised that, as the book puts it, she quite forgot how to speak good English. Carroll loved bending words until they squeaked.

headline: A word is dead when it is said, some say. I say it just begins to live that day.
lesson: Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems and published only a handful in her lifetime. Most were found in her room after she died.

headline: There is no frigate like a book to take us lands away.
lesson: A frigate is a fast sailing ship. Dickinson rarely left her home town, and travelled a long way by reading.

headline: Hope is the thing with feathers that perches in the soul.
lesson: She turns a feeling into a small bird that keeps singing through the storm and never asks for a crumb in return.

headline: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.
lesson: His advice still holds. You do not owe every book the same attention. Skim some, read some, and live with a few.

headline: Reading maketh a full man, conference a ready man, and writing an exact man.
lesson: Conference here means conversation. Read to fill your mind, talk to sharpen it, and write to find out what you really think.

headline: A little learning is a dangerous thing.
connecting: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism
lesson: Often misquoted as a little knowledge. His point was that a small taste makes us overconfident, and deeper study makes us humble again.

headline: To err is human; to forgive, divine.
connecting: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism
lesson: Pope published this at twenty-three, in a poem about how to judge other people’s writing fairly and kindly.

headline: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.
connecting: Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities
lesson: This is only the start of the opening sentence, which runs on for well over a hundred words before it reaches a full stop.

headline: Call me Ishmael.
lesson: Three words, and one of the most famous openings in English. Notice he does not say it is his name, only what to call him.

headline: All the world’s a stage, and all the men and women merely players.
connecting: William Shakespeare, As You Like It
lesson: The speech goes on to split a life into seven ages, from the infant to the very old. Player was the word for an actor.

headline: We are such stuff as dreams are made on.
lesson: Often misquoted as made of. Prospero says it as his magic show melts away, in one of the last plays Shakespeare wrote.

headline: The best words in the best order.
lesson: His full definition was a pair. Prose is words in their best order. Poetry is the best words in the best order.

headline: Words are, of course, the most powerful drug used by mankind.
lesson: Kipling said this in a speech to surgeons in London. He told them that words do not only carry meaning, they change how people feel.

headline: Tell all the truth but tell it slant.
lesson: Her advice is to come at hard truths from the side, gently. The truth, she writes, must dazzle gradually.

headline: typewriter
lesson: On a standard QWERTY keyboard all ten letters sit on the top row. So do the letters of proprietor, perpetuity and repertoire.

headline: rhythm
landing: a, e, i, o or u
lesson: The letter y does the work of a vowel here. Other words that manage without the usual five include myth, lynx, crypt and gym.

headline: uncopyrightable
lesson: A word with no repeated letters is called an isogram. Dermatoglyphics, the study of fingerprints, is another with fifteen.

headline: almost
lesson: So do begin, chimp, ghost and biopsy. Words like this are rare, and the longer the word, the rarer it gets.

headline: bookkeeper
lesson: Double o, double k, double e. Bookkeeper and bookkeeping are the only common English words with three pairs of double letters back to back.

headline: queue
lesson: Take away the last four letters and you still say it the same way. The word is French for tail, which is what a line of people looks like.

headline: the tittle
landing: the dot over i and j
lesson: It comes from the Latin for a small mark. Some people think the phrase to a T began as to a tittle, meaning down to the smallest detail.
Children ended the alphabet with: and, per se, and. Said quickly, that slurred into the word ampersand.

headline: E
lesson: It turns up in roughly one of every eight letters you read. In 1939 Ernest Vincent Wright published Gadsby, a 50,000 word novel without a single e.

headline: the
lesson: It makes up roughly one word in every twenty on a typical page. The top ten also includes be, to, of, and, a and in.

headline: run
lesson: Editors of the Oxford English Dictionary counted 645 senses for the verb run, taking the record from set.

headline: ye olde
lesson: The y stood in for an old letter called thorn, which made the th sound. Printers without a thorn used y, and readers later forgot.

headline: OK
lesson: In 1839 a Boston newspaper used it as a jokey short form of oll korrect, a deliberate misspelling of all correct. It is now understood almost everywhere.

headline: dreamt
lesson: It is the only common English word that does, along with its relatives undreamt and daydreamt.

headline: strengths
lesson: It is among the longest English words with a single vowel, and one of the longest you can say in a single syllable.

headline: pangram
lesson: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog is the famous one. Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow does it in twenty-nine letters.

headline: palindrome
lesson: Level, kayak and racecar all work. So does a whole sentence: A man, a plan, a canal, Panama.

headline: your eyes
lesson: They jump. Each hop is called a saccade, and you only take in words during the short pauses in between, a few letters at a time.

headline: one in ten
lesson: Dyslexia mainly affects reading and spelling. It has nothing to do with intelligence, and many dyslexic people are strong visual and creative thinkers.

headline: octothorpe
lesson: Engineers at Bell Labs are said to have coined it in the 1960s for the telephone keypad. Octo is for its eight points.

headline: a murmuration
connecting: is the word for a flock of
lesson: Thousands of starlings turn together in the evening sky like one shape. The name copies the murmur of all those wings.

headline: an exaltation
connecting: is the word for a flock of
lesson: It comes from a hunting book printed in 1486, the Book of Saint Albans, which also lists a murder of crows and a pride of lions.

headline: a flamboyance
connecting: is the word for a group of
lesson: Flamingo and flamboyant both go back to words for flame. The birds get their pink from the shrimp and algae they eat.

headline: break the ice
lesson: Small boats broke river ice so that trade could start again. By the 1600s it also meant easing the first awkward moments between strangers.

headline: once in a blue moon
lesson: Today a blue moon usually means a second full moon in one calendar month. That happens about once every two or three years.

headline: spill the beans
lesson: It appeared in American slang in the early 1900s. The story about ancient Greeks voting with beans is a nice one, but there is no proof.

headline: under the weather
lesson: It is probably a sailor’s phrase. A seasick sailor was sent below deck, out of the weather, to recover.

headline: bite the bullet
lesson: The story goes that soldiers bit on a bullet during surgery without anaesthetic. Kipling used the phrase in a novel in 1891.

headline: affect or effect?
lesson: Rain affects your mood. Rain has an effect on your mood. If you can put the or an in front of it, you want effect.

headline: stationary or stationery?
connecting: the one with an e is for
lesson: Stationery with an e is paper, pens and envelopes. Stationary with an a means standing still, like a parked car.

headline: their, there, they’re
lesson: Their shows belonging. There points to a place. They’re is short for they are. Say they are out loud, and if it fits, use the apostrophe.

headline: lose or loose?
lesson: You lose your keys. A loose tooth wobbles. Lose rhymes with choose, and loose rhymes with goose.

headline: desert or dessert?
lesson: A desert is dry sand. Dessert is pudding. To desert someone, with the stress on the end, is to abandon them.

headline: complement or compliment?
lesson: Complement shares its first six letters with complete. A compliment with an i is the kind thing that I say to you.

headline: she sells seashells
lesson: Tongue twisters work by packing nearly identical sounds together, here s and sh, so your tongue has to keep switching between them.

headline: red lorry, yellow lorry
lesson: The sounds r and l are made with the tongue in almost the same place, so swapping quickly between them trips nearly everybody up.

headline: Peter Piper
lesson: The rhyme was printed in London in 1813 in a book of tongue twisters, one for each letter of the alphabet. A peck is about nine litres.

headline: the whole nine yards
lesson: Nobody knows where it comes from. Guesses include cloth, concrete and machine-gun belts, and none of them has been proved.

headline: principal or principle?
lesson: A principal is the head of a school, or the main thing. A principle is a rule or a belief that you stick to.

headline: onomatopoeia
lesson: Buzz, hiss, splash, cuckoo, murmur. The name is Greek for making a name, and it is much harder to spell than any of its examples.
